# Welcome {.unnumbered}

This is the course text for **Factory Physics Through Factorio**: a sequence
of laboratory experiments in which you operate, measure, and redesign real
(simulated) production systems, and meet the formal theory only *after* you
have experienced the phenomenon it explains.

The laboratory is [FISL](https://github.com/MetaCoding-io/FactorioResearch)
— the Factorio Industrial Systems Laboratory. Factorio provides the physics
of production: machines, belts, buffers, recipes, power. FISL provides the
experimental apparatus around it: controlled material supply, declared
system boundaries, an exact experiment clock, and measurement whose every
number carries its method, window, and validity.

The governing idea:

> **Use Factorio to model the system. Use FISL to model the experiment.**

## How the labs work

Each lab follows the same protocol:

1. **Encounter** a deliberately constructed production system.
2. **Run** a controlled, timed experiment while it operates (or while you
   modify it).
3. **Read the report** — reproducible measurements, not impressions.
4. **Meet the theory** that names what you observed.
5. **Intervene and re-run**, then compare attempts side by side.

Every run you perform produces an auditable record; two runs of the same
scenario are exactly comparable, and the deterministic simulation means a
repeated run without intervention reproduces its numbers *exactly*. Your
experiments are experiments in the scientific sense.

Between labs, short **interludes** develop the theory the phenomena have
earned: each one builds only on what earlier labs made you measure, and
each ends with claims stated precisely enough to be wrong — which the
next lab then tests. Theory here is never an announcement; it is a
hypothesis you are about to check against a system you can walk around
in.

## What this course assumes

No Factorio experience is required — but that promise is kept by the
*Before the First Lab* chapter, not by wishful thinking: it teaches the
handful of controls the course uses (there are about a dozen), the
plant-floor reading of the game's objects, and the one-time setup. Start
there if you've never played. No mathematics beyond arithmetic is
required to *do* the labs; the interludes introduce each formal
relationship as it is earned.

## What the simulation assumes away {.unnumbered}

Factorio's machines execute perfectly, never fail, and hide nothing. Real
factories — and real organizations — do none of these things. Each lab ends
by stating explicitly what the simulation represented, what it omitted, and
which conclusions are (and are not) warranted. Treat that discipline as part
of the subject: knowing the limits of a model is what makes it usable.
